title: Maryland says ‘Leave no one behind.’ So, why are young adults still invisible?
summary: When it comes to inclusion for young adults with chronic conditions, Maryland has studied the issue, documented it and adopted policies on it, writes Santi Bhagat. But it lags when it comes to executing, leaving many "Young Invisibles" feeling left out.
content:
by Santi Bhagat, Maryland Matters March 15, 2026

by Santi Bhagat, Maryland Matters March 15, 2026

When I read about Gov. Wes Moore’s $5 million apprenticeship initiative, I thought this would be perfect for young adults with chronic health conditions. Sadly, they were not included.

Moore and Lt. Gov. Aruna Miller won in 2022 promising to Leave No One Behind. They’re running on it again for 2026. One in three young adults lives with a chronic childhood condition, and they’ve been left behind their entire adult lives. Many call themselves Young Invisibles.

After my daughter became ill at age 8, I founded a nonprofit that discovered a void of supports when young people with chronic conditions turn 18. Medical advances allowed many millennials to survive conditions into adulthood — triumphs we did not plan for. These still-developing young adults find there is no field of young adult medicine and few supports in education and work.

As a physician-parent, I know firsthand how dire things are. Even with medical knowledge, good insurance and networks, I could not help my daughter. At 38, she feels like a failure after dropping out of college – with a 3.6 GPA – and unable to find a path to employment.

Her story is not unique. Too often, I hear how Young Invisibles struggle to secure health care, manage college and work. Families find they have to figure this out on their own, not realizing this is a systems failure.

Maryland was the first to act. In 2006, Majority Leader Kumar Barve pioneered legislation on quality health care for children with special health care needs. In 2018, then-Del. Aruna Miller introduced the nation’s first bill on higher education for students with chronic conditions. In 2021, Speaker Joseline Pena-Melnyk, then a delegate, and Sen. Brian Feldman advanced legislation that resulted in a report with 17 recommendations. U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen has championed this issue since 2004 and introduced a joint resolution with Rep. Jamie Raskin in 2023.

Maryland didn’t miss the problem. Maryland named it. Studied it. Documented it. Maryland is positioned to lead the nation IF it explicitly includes Young Invisibles in the American Dream.

Consider education: Colleges send Young Invisibles to disability offices that are not designed for chronic absenteeism or medical instability. They need specific accommodations and health support. University of Maryland officials testified in 2022 that one case manager would be insufficient as they have up to 10,000 students with chronic conditions.

What does that mean? UMd collects tuition from these students. Promises opportunities. Then admits they lack the infrastructure to support them.

Data plays a huge role in keeping them invisible. Institutions do not track Young Invisibles; policymakers can’t respond to problems that are not measured.

The governor’s apprenticeship initiative repeats this blind spot — it assumes fixed schedules, consistent attendance. Health-informed job coaching could help young adults overcome these barriers. But only if we acknowledge they exist.

Millennials and Gen Z comprise half the workforce. When Young Invisibles can’t complete college or sustain employment, costs land on families, public programs, the economy.

What troubles me most is that we had to make the economic case. For decades, families have raised moral concerns, with little effect. Only when framing this as an economic risk, do people pay attention. Are our leaders more compelled to protect the economy than vulnerable young adults?

Many Maryland leaders are excited to be the first changemakers. But they must execute. Continued inaction is not neutral. If Maryland doesn’t act, it knowingly keeps Young Invisibles in a policy black hole.

The path forward is clear. Implement the 2021 higher-education recommendations. Include Young Invisibles explicitly in apprenticeship programs and advisory roles. Establish the nation’s first Governor’s Cabinet for Young Adult Health—coordinating policy across health, education, workforce, social services. Create a model not just for Young Invisibles but for other vulnerable young adults.

A governor-led convening of college presidents, health leaders, employers could confront this directly. Maryland’s academic medical centers are positioned to lead national progress linking young adult health, education, employment.

When this work began in 2009, the oldest millennials were 28. They’re 45 now. An entire generation passed through young adulthood without support.

Our nation has a fiduciary responsibility for Young Invisibles. Maryland has all the elements to be the role model.

The promise was Leave No One Behind. Young Invisibles are still waiting. I hear from them—and their families—every week.

I hope our leaders are listening too.
